title: A Charleston tour guide has gathered paranormal photos for years. He's giving us a closer look.
excerpt: Explore mysterious images captured during the Ghosts of Charleston tour in the historic downtown district.
content:
Editor's note: All photographs and claims accompanying this story were provided by tour guide Simon Martineau. The newspaper has not independently verified the claims nor altered the images.

There are some spirits whose fortune, fate or circumstance has them tethered to this world.

Why? We cannot be sure. Is there some unfinished business? Or are they possibly here as a guide for the living?

We don't always see them. We don't always hear them. But if we allow ourselves, we may sense that their presence, their legacy and their imprint can affect us profoundly.

These are local tour guide Simon Martineau’s opening words for the Ghosts of Charleston Tour that takes guests on a serene yet spooky stroll through the Unitarian Church graveyard and Philadelphia Alley in the downtown historic district, among other sites.

You become a ghost hunter on this tour, he said, so feel free to take pictures of any and everything, but be sure to turn off the flash — because the spirit world does not like it.

For the last six and half years, Martineau has recounted ghost stories from Charleston author Julian Buxton’s 26-year-old book “The Ghosts of Charleston” as he takes guests between sacred sites permeated with generational memory and emotion.

“I have a deep connection to the spirit world,” said Martineau, who was born and raised in England before moving to the U.S. in 1987. He moved to Charleston 19 years ago when he retired from a 20-year career playing professional polo.

“I also have a reverence for the characters in the stories because they were real people and suffered just like we suffer,” he said. “This in itself creates humility and empathy within me. It is a wonderful spiritual journey, and I feel truly blessed to be a part of it.”

Unexplained encounters

If you happen to snap a paranormal photo Martineau wants to collect, he asks that you send the photo to him while still on the tour to ensure it isn’t altered.

The phenomena he’s collected from his tour guests range from distinctive dark figures, silky substances and misty apparitions to celestial light, floating orbs and swirling portals.

In one photo, a phantom appears to be seated in the bed of a truck parked out front of the St. Phillip's Episcopal Church Cemetery on Church Street. Martineau believes it to be the ghost of John C. Calhoun, who is buried there.

In another, a floating figure seems to appear in front of a tour guest seated in the Unitarian Church graveyard near a mass grave, known as a pauper's grave, which is a particularly active area for encounters, Martineau said.

In one photo captured at Philadelphia Alley, considered one of the most haunted spots downtown, a guest snapped a photo of what Martineau believes is a portal — a multidimensional tunnel or entrance to a parallel plane of existence.

Philadelphia Alley

During the tour, when he leads you through the brick-laden alley, Martineau encourages you to look closely for handprints found on the bricks left by enslaved children who handled them during manufacturing.

Also known as “Bloody Alley” or “Dueler's Alley” for the many duels fought there until the practice was outlawed in 1880, Philadelphia Alley is your backdrop as Martineau tells you the tragic love story of the “Whistling Ghost.”

Joseph Brown Ladd, who moved to Charleston in 1783, fell in love with a woman named Amanda. He was killed in the alley after his friend challenged him to a duel, envious of the successful, happy life he led. Indeed, Joseph was known to whistle as he cut through the alley on his way to work.

It is said that you can hear a faint whistling there to this day.

Spiritual energy

Martineau has developed an ability to feel the paranormal presence, he said, almost like sensing humid air from dry air.

“Spiritual energy manifests to me like a warm silk-like texture,” he said. “It’s quite viscous.”

Buxton Books owner Polly Buxton, who’s known Martineau for over 20 years, said there’s just something special about him.

“He’s one of the most gifted storytellers I’ve ever worked with,” said Buxton, whose husband wrote “The Ghosts of Charleston” all those years ago.

“His guests seem to have more than their share of unexplained encounters in the Unitarian graveyard,” she said. “I can’t tell you why. I think some things are better left to mystery and wonder.”

Graveyard gazing

When you enter the Unitarian Church graveyard, what Martineau calls “a veritable Eden,” you’re overcome by the lusciousness of the shrubs and trees growing among the grave plots — live oaks, palmetto palms, crepe myrtles, cedar, holly.

The graveyard itself seems to assure you death isn’t the end of anything, he said.

Being surrounded by lush foliage and wisps of wind, there’s a predominant sense of peace that floats about.

If you’re lucky, you’ll encounter a friendly black-and-white street cat nicknamed Poe, who enjoys accompanying the tour guests.

Martineau begins with the story of Mary and Edward Whitridge of Mount Pleasant, who are the subjects of a well-known Holy City ghost story.

Mary passed away on Jan. 23, 1907, and was laid to rest in the graveyard in her family's plot. She died of heart failure the same day her husband, Edward, died while traveling by ship to Baltimore to receive care for his ill health.

Because he was buried in Baltimore, the plot right next to Mary in the Unitarian churchyard remains empty to this day, and local folklore claims her spirit walks the graveyard looking for her husband.

One of Martineau's guests captured a photo of a figure he believes to be Mary near her gravestone, and he added it to his collection.

As you carry on about the tour, you can’t help but let down your guard as Martineau speaks on behalf of those long passed. 

A woman named Maureen Ann Kelleher took his tour recently and shared that she is clairvoyant — a person who is said to possess the extrasensory ability to perceive information, visual images, symbols or future events that cannot be gathered through normal physical senses.

“From what I experienced, (he) appeared to be channeling the narratives directly from the spirit realm,” said Kelleher, who Martineau calls an “oracle.”

“(His) storytelling legitimately brought to life the experiences, hopes and sensibilities of the disincarnate,” she said.

The beauty of a good ghost story is that reality bears no weight. You are free to believe.
